### Part A — Examples of Conditional Statements


```{r}
# Example A: if ... else. Choose between two outcomes for a single value.

score <- 78

if (score >= 75) {
  print("Passed")
} else {
  print("Failed")
}

```

```{r}
# Example B: if ... else if ... else. Use it when there are more than two outcomes.

score <- 86

if (score >= 90) {
  print("Excellent")
} else if (score >= 80) {
  print("Good")
} else if (score >= 75) {
  print("Fair")
} else {
  print("Needs Improvement")
}

```

```{r}
# Example C: ifelse() for a whole vector.

scores <- c(92, 68, 75, 81, 59)

ifelse(scores >= 75, "Passed", "Failed")

```

```{r}
# Example D: combining conditions.

grade <- 91
attendance <- 95

if (grade >= 90 & attendance >= 90) {
  print("Honors candidate")
}

```


### Part B — Conditional Statements


# Question #1:

```{r}
# Set temp <- 33. Print "Hot" if temp is 32 or higher, otherwise print "Not hot"

temp <- 33

if (temp >= 32) {
  print("Hot")
} else {
  print("Not hot")
}

```


# Question #2:

```{r}
# Set age <- 17. Use if ... else if ... else to print "Child" for ages below 13, "Teenager" for 13 to 19, and "Adult" for 20 and above.

age <- 17

if (age < 13) {
  print("Child")
} else if (age <= 19) {
  print("Teenager")
} else {
  print("Adult")
}

```


# Question #3:

```{r}
# Create marks <- c(45, 88, 73, 100, 62). Use ifelse() to create a vector result that says "Pass" for marks of 60 or higher and "Fail" otherwise. Print result.

marks <- c(45, 88, 73, 100, 62)
result <- ifelse(marks >= 60, "Pass", "Fail")
result

```


# Question #4:

```{r}
# Predict the output of the code below before you run it. Then run it and explain, in a comment, why you got that result.

# Prediction: "A"

x <- 10
if (x > 5) {
  print("A")
} else if (x > 8) {
  print("B")
} else {
  print("C")
}

# Explanation:
# R checks conditions from top to bottom and stops at the first TRUE one. Since 10 is already greater than 5, it prints "A" and skips the rest.

```


# Question #5:

```{r}
# What is the difference between if and ifelse()? When would you choose each one?

# Explanation:
# if checks only one single value at a time, while ifelse() checks every item in a whole vector at once.
# Use if when making decisions on a single value (like checking if a file exists), and use ifelse() when creating or updating a whole column in a table.

```


### Part C: Importing the CSV File


# Question #6:

```{r}
# a. Import the file safely.

grades <- read.csv("students_grades.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

```

```{r}
# b. Use if ... else to check that the file exists before importing it.

if (file.exists("students_grades.csv")) {
  grades <- read.csv("students_grades.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  print("File loaded!")
} else {
  print("File not found.")
}

```

```{r}
# c. Inspect the data.

# first 6 rows
head(grades)

# number of rows and columns
dim(grades)

# column names and data types
str(grades)

# basic statistics per column
summary(grades)

# number of missing values per column
colSums(is.na(grades))

```

```{r}
# d. Answer the following:

nrow(grades); ncol(grades)
colSums(is.na(grades))
class(grades$Section)
range(grades$Attendance)

# Answers:
# 1. grades has 15 rows and 7 columns.
# 2. The Midterm column is the only one with a missing value (NA), and it has exactly 1.
# 3. Section is a character (text) column, because it holds the labels A, B, and C.
# 4. The lowest Attendance is the first number printed by range(grades$Attendance), and the highest is the second.
#    (Write them here after knitting: lowest = ___, highest = ___.)

```

```{r}
# e. Check the grades should have 15 rows, 7 columns, and exactly one NA.

nrow(grades) == 15
ncol(grades) == 7
sum(is.na(grades)) == 1

```

```{r}
# f. Applying Conditional Statements

# f.1 Compute the final grade.
grades$FinalGrade <- 0.30 * grades$Quiz + 0.30 * grades$Midterm + 0.40 * grades$Final
grades$FinalGrade

```

```{r}
# f.2 Pass or fail. Check for NA first, because NA >= 75 gives NA, not TRUE or FALSE.

grades$Result <- ifelse(is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Incomplete",
                        ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 75, "Passed", "Failed"))
grades$Result

```

```{r}
# f.3 Grade remarks.

grades$Remarks <- ifelse(is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Incomplete",
                  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 90, "Excellent",
                  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 85, "Very Good",
                  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 80, "Good",
                  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 75, "Fair", "Needs Improvement")))))
grades$Remarks

```

```{r}
# f.4 Attendance flag.

grades$AttendanceFlag <- ifelse(grades$Attendance < 80, "At Risk", "OK")
grades$AttendanceFlag

```

```{r}
# f.5 Honors candidates.

grades$Honors <- ifelse(!is.na(grades$FinalGrade) & grades$FinalGrade >= 90 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Yes", "No")
grades$Honors

```

```{r}
# f.6 if ... else if inside a loop.

loop_result <- character(nrow(grades))

for (i in 1:nrow(grades)) {
  if (is.na(grades$FinalGrade[i])) {
    loop_result[i] <- "Incomplete"
  } else if (grades$FinalGrade[i] >= 75) {
    loop_result[i] <- "Passed"
  } else {
    loop_result[i] <- "Failed"
  }
}

loop_result

```

```{r}
# f.7 Now try if (grades$FinalGrade >= 75) print("Passed") on its own in the Console. Explain the error or warning R gives and why the loop version avoids it.

# Explanation:
# R gives the error "the condition has length > 1" (older R versions only gave a warning and used the first element).
# A plain if needs one TRUE or FALSE, but grades$FinalGrade >= 75 produces 15 values at once.
# The loop version avoids this because grades$FinalGrade[i] picks one student per turn, so each if gets a single value.

```

```{r}
# f.8 Summarize your results.

table(grades$Result)
table(grades$AttendanceFlag)
table(grades$Honors)

sum(grades$Result == "Passed")
sum(grades$AttendanceFlag == "At Risk")
sum(grades$Honors == "Yes")

# Summary (replace each ___ with the number printed above after knitting):
# Passed: ___ students
# At Risk: ___ students
# Honors candidates: ___ students
# The one student with the missing midterm is counted as "Incomplete," not as Passed or Failed.

```

```{r}
# f.9 Check grades should now have 12 columns (7 original plus FinalGrade, Result, Remarks, AttendanceFlag, Honors).

ncol(grades)
names(grades)

```


### Part D: Exporting Results to .csv


# Question #7:

```{r}
# a. Export the full processed table.

write.csv(grades, "students_grades_processed.csv", row.names = FALSE)

```

```{r}
# b. Export the at-risk students. The file is written only when there is at least one at-risk student.

at_risk <- grades[grades$AttendanceFlag == "At Risk", ]

if (nrow(at_risk) > 0) {
  write.csv(at_risk, "at_risk_students.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  print("at_risk_students.csv exported.")
} else {
  print("No at-risk students found.")
}

```

```{r}
# c. Export the honors list.

honors <- grades[!is.na(grades$Honors) & grades$Honors == "Yes",
                 c("StudentID", "Name", "Section", "FinalGrade", "Attendance")]

if (nrow(honors) > 0) {
  write.csv(honors, "honors_list.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  print("honors_list.csv exported.")
} else {
  print("No honors candidates found.")
}

```

```{r}
# d. Verify your exports. Never assume a file was written correctly. Read it back and compare.

check_processed <- read.csv("students_grades_processed.csv")
head(check_processed)
dim(check_processed)

```


# Question #8:

```{r}
# 1. How does the missing midterm appear in the exported file?
# 2. What would the file look like without row.names = FALSE? Try it with a temporary file name and compare.

write.csv(grades, "temp_test.csv")
head(read.csv("temp_test.csv"))

# Answers:
# 1. The missing midterm is written as the text NA in the exported file, so the student's Midterm and FinalGrade cells both show NA.
# 2. Without row.names = FALSE, R adds an extra first column of row numbers (1, 2, 3, ...). When the file is read back, that column appears as "X",
#    so the file has 13 columns instead of the 12 it should have.

```


# Question #9:

```{r}
# a & b. Add a column Scholarship to grades using nested ifelse() statements. Test the missing grade first, then Full, then Partial.

grades$Scholarship <- ifelse(is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Pending",
                      ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 95 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Full",
                      ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 85 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Partial", "None")))

```

```{r}
# c. Select students whose Scholarship is "Full" or "Partial".

scholarship_candidates <- grades[grades$Scholarship %in% c("Full", "Partial"), ]
scholarship_candidates

```

```{r}
# d. Export them to scholarship_candidates.csv with row.names = FALSE, using an if ... else guard.

if (nrow(scholarship_candidates) > 0) {
  write.csv(scholarship_candidates, "scholarship_candidates.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  print("scholarship_candidates.csv saved.")
} else {
  print("No scholarship candidates found.")
}

```

# Question #10:

```{r}
# Question #10
# Answer in one or two sentences each, as comments.
# 1. Why did you check is.na() before comparing the final grade to a number?
# 2. In Task 3.2, what would happen if the Failed condition were placed before the Incomplete condition?
# 3. When is ifelse() the better choice than if ... else, and when is if ... else better?
# 4. Why is it useful to read an exported CSV back into R?

# Answers:
# 1. R cannot compare a missing value (NA) to a number, so the result is NA instead of TRUE or FALSE. Checking is.na() first catches the incomplete grade
#    before it can make a later comparison, or an if statement, fail.
# 2. The student with the missing midterm would get NA in the Result column instead of "Incomplete," because NA >= 75 is NA and never reaches the label.
# 3. ifelse() is better when you test a whole column or vector at once, such as creating a new column. if ... else is better when you test one
#    single value, such as whether a file exists or whether a list is empty.
# 4. Reading the exported CSV back confirms the file was written correctly. It shows whether the NA values, the column count, and the extra row-number column came out as expected.

```
